---
title: "DMSTAr: A Reproducible R Framework for Network-Based Simulation of Hydrology and Phosphorus Dynamics in Treatment Wetlands"
date: "2026-09-23"
abstract: >
  Wetland water quality models are central to evaluating phosphorus (P) removal and restoration planning in managed landscapes such as the Florida Everglades. The Dynamic Model for Stormwater Treatment Areas (DMSTA), a legacy spreadsheet/VBA implementation limits transparency, reproducibility, and integration with other workflows. We developed DMSTAr, an open-source R implementation that preserves DMSTA equations, numerical procedures, routing logic, and version-specific behavior within a modular, testable framework. We verified DMSTAr against legacy outputs using identical inputs, parameters, initial conditions, and network structures from four major Everglades planning applications. Agreement was evaluated using bias, median absolute difference, root-mean-square error, symmetric percent difference, and graphical diagnostics. DMSTAr reproduced legacy behavior with negligible systematic bias and high agreement across applications. DMSTA and DMSTAr also exhibited nearly identical sensitivity to integration step size. DMSTAr therefore provides a faithful, reproducible, extensible, accessible and adaptable implementation of DMSTA for scenario analysis, diagnostic evaluation, and long-term wetland water-quality modeling.

# Introduction

Wetlands are biogeochemical hotspots that regulate water quality through coupled hydrologic, biological and geochemical processes that influence nutrient retention, transformation and export [@chapraSurfaceWaterqualityModeling1997; @chengBiogeochemicalHotspotsRole2017; @kadlecTreatmentWetlands2009; @rabaeyFreshwaterBiogeochemicalHotspots2024; @reddyBiogeochemistryWetlandsScience2008]. Given this functionality, natural, restored and constructed or treatment wetlands have been used as water quality treatment systems for nutrient and contaminant removal [@kadlecTreatmentWetlands2009; @wuConstructedWetlandsPollution2023]. As such, approaches to modeling these dynamic systems have evolved over time.

Modeling approaches for wetland water quality have evolved from empirical, statistical and steady-state design equations toward dynamic mass-balance and process-informed biogeochemical models [@kadlecLargeConstructedWetlands2016; @kadlecAutobioticWetlandPhosphorus1997; @lariosEffectsIncreasingComplexity2024; @walkerModelingPhosphorusDynamics2011]. Early phosphorus (P) modeling in the freshwater marshes of the Florida Everglades demonstrated that long-term P uptake could be characterized by using first-order areal rate relationships coupled with water, soil and biotic compartment mass balances. This led to ecosystem level models that included explicit representations of wetland P storage, recycling, sedimentation, vegetation, and hydrologic forcing [@walkerModelingPhosphorusDynamics2011].

In the Everglades, P models have been critical in restoration planning efforts due to the need for water quality protection and the ensure that the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan achieve its core objectives of restoring Quality, Quantity, Timing and Distribution of water to the Everglades [@sklarEcologicalSocietalUnderpinnings2005]. Everglades P modeling progressed from continuously stirring tank reactor steady-state design models for Stormwater Treatment Areas (STA) to gradient and dynamic simulation tools used to simulate system performance. The Dynamic Model for Stormwater Treatment Areas (DMSTA) was developed along this model continuum as a parsimonious dynamic extension of earlier P-k-C\* or Tank-in-Series models that incorporate hydrologic routing and labile P storage to represent event-driven treatment wetland behavior [@kadlecLimitsPhosphorusRemoval1999; @kadlecTreatmentWetlands2009; @walkerModelingPhosphorusDynamics2011].

The objective of this study was not to assess the rigor or limitations of the DMSTA methodology [@justonTechnicalSupportDMSTA2016; @justonDatadrivenModelingPhosphorus2019; @kadlecEvergladesWaterQuality2026; @paudelDoesIncreasedModel2012], but to develop a transparent network-based implementation and verify fidelity against established applications and demonstrate analyses. Specifically, DMSTA was translated into a modular set of functions distributed as the \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} `R` package. While the original DMSTA implementation relies on VBA code integrated with an extensive spreadsheet environment, \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} was developed to enhance transparency, reproducibility, extensibility, accessible and adaptable. In contrast to spreadsheet based models, where logic is distributed across dispersed and often opaque formulas, the coded workflow explicitly defines all equations, assumptions, and data transformations. This design enables systematic interrogation of intermediate model states, formal version control, scalable scenario analysis, and consistent application across multiple systems. Consequently, \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} serves not only as an execution engine for DMSTA equivalent simulations, but as a reproducible modeling framework suitable for comparison, extension, and long term scientific application.

This study is limited to demonstrating parity between the original DMSTA implementation and its translation into the R based \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} framework. The comparison emphasizes equivalence in equations, parameterization, and outputs, rather than evaluation of model assumptions, calibration, or predictive performance. Although \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} provides a modular and extensible architecture, only those components required to reproduce DMSTA behavior are considered here. Potential extensions enabled by the R framework are acknowledged but are outside the scope of this work.

# Methods

## Model Translation and Software Architecture

\CRANpkg{DMSTAr} is an open source R implementation of the DMSTA, designed to reproduce the numerical behavior of existing spreadsheet based DMSTA releases while providing a transparent, extensible modeling framework [@zotero-item-2162]. Rather than attempting to harmonize algorithmic behavior across historical DMSTA versions, \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} explicitly preserves hydrologic and hydraulic semantics and conceptual units (Table `r knitr::asis_output('\\@ref(tab:Tab1-tab)')`).

```{r Table1_dat}
Tab1_dat_ls <- vector("list",6)
Tab1_dat_ls[[1]] <- data.frame(
  Term = c("Series"),Definition = c("A time ordered data frame containing daily model forcings (e.g., inflow discharge, inflow concentration, rainfall, evapotranspiration, operational releases) used to drive simulations.")
)
Tab1_dat_ls[[2]] <- data.frame(
  Term = c("Cell"),Definition = c("The fundamental spatial unit representing an individual treatment or storage area with its own hydrologic and phosphorus mass balances.")
)
Tab1_dat_ls[[3]] <- data.frame(
  Term = c("Case"),Definition = c("A collection of one or more cells simulated together under a shared input series and parameter set, corresponding to a single model configuration.")
)
Tab1_dat_ls[[4]] <- data.frame(
  Term = c("Network"),Definition = c("A hydrologically connected set of cases or cells in which outflows from upstream elements are routed to downstream elements.")
)
Tab1_dat_ls[[5]] <- data.frame(
  Term = c("Splitter"),Definition = c("A designated routing element that partitions inflow or treated outflow among downstream cells or cases according to specified fractions.")
)
Tab1_dat_ls[[6]] <- data.frame(
  Term = c("Tank"),Definition = c("A cell segment used in simulating mass transport using the tanks-in-series model")
)
Tab1_dat <- do.call(rbind,Tab1_dat_ls)
```

The current release version of the \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} package is available as an open-source R package and has been published on Comprehensive R Archive Network [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/DMSTAr). The current release and development version source code are also maintained in a [Github repository](https://github.com/SwampThingPaul/DMSTAr). The repository provides full access to source code, documentation, vignettes and example workflows to support reproducibility. This repository does not contain DMSTA source code and/or published DMSTA results evaluated in this manuscript. The DMSTA model files and associated output results for each project evaluated in this study are available through a permanent data repository [@zotero-item-2162].

The \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} package was developed through a systematic translation of the legacy DMSTA Microsoft Excel workbook and associated Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) code into a modular, function based `R` implementation. Rather than performing a line by line code conversion, model development focused on preserving the original governing equations, numerical integration scheme, and execution logic while restructuring the model into explicit, reusable components. Additionally, spreadsheet‑based calculations that relied on implicit cell dependencies were reformulated as explicit state‑space updates within R functions, making intermediate states and fluxes directly accessible for diagnostics and testing. This approach improves transparency, reproducibility, and extensibility while maintaining conceptual and numerical consistency with the original DMSTA framework.

To ensure flexibility and legacy implementation, \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} supports multiple DMSTA version semantics through an explicit model configuration parameter. This parameter governs algorithmic features that materially affect simulated hydrology, including rules for release gating, depth control, and inflow fraction handling. Under the default configuration corresponding to DMSTA Version 2E, releases are subject only to depth based gating and specified discharge constraints, consistent with published release behavior. Meanwhile, consistent with DMSTA Version 2C2B, an alternative release-gating logic and offline/resting-period behavior was included. The alternative release-gating logic in Version 2C2B uses a negative minimum release-depth parameter to activate a hydraulic constraint on specified releases. Under this option, the absolute value of the parameter is used as the release-depth threshold, but prescribed releases are limited to the available overland-flow capacity calculated from the simulated water depth and outflow-rating relationship. The offline function represents periodic operational resting of selected treatment flow paths by modifying inflow allocation during a scheduled offline window. When activated, the model replaces the default cell inflow fraction with a prescribed offline-period fraction for a 45-day period beginning March 15 and recurring every three years. The offline period does not suspend model calculations; hydrologic and phosphorus state variables continue to evolve through the standard time-stepping routine while external routing conditions are temporarily altered. After the resting window, the model returns to the baseline inflow allocation.

At its core, DMSTA is based on a hydrologic and P mass balance formulated as a first order ordinary differential equation (ODE) that governs total water volume, P transfer and storage across compartments. The original DMSTA implementation applies state dependent constraints and flux corrections in an order dependent manner. Earlier versions of DMSTA include Euler integration and later Runge-Kutta (RK4) integration methods. To preserve fidelity with DMSTA, \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} can implement both Euler and RK4 integration methods. For future applications, Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg (RKF45) and an option for custom ODE solvers were included in the current version of \CRANpkg{DMSTAr}; however, these were not evaluated as part of this manuscript. 

Model functionality was developed hierarchically at three organizational scales, reflecting the original DMSTA conceptual structure. First, core functions were implemented to simulate hydrology and TP dynamics within a single treatment cell. These functions encapsulate daily water balance calculations, phosphorus mass balances, and sub daily numerical integration previously embedded across spreadsheet formulas and VBA routines. Second, single cell functions were composed into case level simulations, enabling coordinated execution of multiple cells with shared forcings and parameter sets. Finally, case level simulations were extended to support networked configurations, allowing upstream–downstream connectivity, flow routing, and mass transfer among multiple cases. 

At each level of development, model outputs were compared against the legacy DMSTA spreadsheet for identical input time series and parameter sets to verify numerical equivalence. This staged translation ensured that differences between implementations reflect software architecture rather than changes in model formulation.

## Package Package design and workflow
\CRANpkg{DMSTAr} is structured to support the complete workflow of regional treatment wetland simulations, from model configuration to scenario evaluation. 

Its functionality can be organized into the following workflow stages: 

1. Input data

    * Read input data into R environment sing base functions like `read.csv()` or other packages that handle excel (i.e., `readxl::read_xlsx`)
    
2. Model configuation
    
    * Specify input parameters, `dmsta_default_params()`
    
    *	Validate input parameters, `validate_P_paramsK()`
    
    *	Partitions a single cell area into a series of conceptual tanks used by DMSTA, `dmsta_build_tanks()`
    
    * Build P kinetics slots, `build_P_kin_slots()`
    
    * Initializes per-state state vectors, `dmsta_p_init_state()`
    
    *	Construct cell definitions, `dmsta_make_cell()`
    
    * Validate and normalize cell definitions, `dmsta_validate_cells()`

3.	Simulation execution

    * Cell level simulation hydrology and phosphorus dynamics over a multi-day time series for a single cell, `dmsta_flowP_series() `
    
    * Case level simulation with coupled hydrology and phosphorus dynamics for a network of interconnected DMSTA cells over a daily time series, `dmsta_flowP_case()`
    
    *	Case-level network routing, `build_routes_from_net_table()`
    
    *	Case-level network simulation of coupled hydrology and phosphorus dynamics in topological order (upstream to downstream), `run_network_of_cases()`

The functions in this R-package enable users to transition seamlessly from input data to model configuration and simulation. The package functions lend themselves to support both research applications (i.e., sensitivity and uncertainty analyses) and management or planning-oriented workflows (i.e., scenario testing and performance evaluation).

## Verification and Comparability 

Verification of the \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} implementation was conducted through direct comparison with the legacy DMSTA Excel/VBA model using identical input time series, parameter sets, and initial conditions. Verification focused on numerical equivalence rather than recalibration or structural modification of P kinetics. Comparisons were performed at multiple organizational scales, including single‑cell, case‑level, and networked simulations, to ensure numerical equivalence across the full model hierarchy. Daily outputs for hydrologic states (e.g., depth, volume, discharge) and P metrics (e.g., concentration, mass, and load) were evaluated using visual inspection. Annual (water year; May – April) summarized discharge, load and flow-weighted mean data between \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} and the legacy DMSTA implement was evaluated using signed bias (\CRANpkg{DMSTAr} – DMSTA), median absolute difference, root-mean-square error (RMSE), and symmetric percent differences (Supplemental Table S1). To quantify the typical magnitude of implementation differences while giving greater weight to larger deviations, RMSE was included. Because annual metrics differed in scale and units, RMSE was interpreted within each variable and supplemented with percent-difference summaries, DMSTA by \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} plots (with 1:1 line) and Bland–Altman-style plots [@blandStatisticalMethodsAssessing1986].

Comparability testing were conducted using project scale simulation outputs developed for the Restoration Strategies (RS), Central Everglades Planning Project (CEPP), and Western Everglades Planning Project (WERP) [@zotero-item-2162]. These projects represent independent, operational applications of the legacy DMSTA model spanning a range of hydrologic regimes, network configurations, and management objectives. For each project, \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} simulations were driven using the same time series inputs, parameter values, and network structures used in the corresponding legacy DMSTA analyses, without recalibration or modification. This approach ensured that model comparisons reflect differences in software implementation rather than project specific tuning, and that \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} performance is evaluated under realistic, decision support modeling conditions.

## Numerical Sensitivity and Stability
To evaluate whether the R implementation (i.e.,  \CRANpkg{DMSTAr}) reproduced the numerical behavior of the original spreadsheet/VBA model (i.e., DMSTA), we conducted a limited step-size sensitivity analysis for a representative STA (STA 3/4 in the CEPP) over a 10-year (Jan 1966 – Dec 1976) simulation period. Model runs were repeated using 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 integration steps per day with 4 steps per day representing the resolution used in the originally published model application [@sfwmdCentralEvergladesPlanning2018] and therefore the reference value for comparison. Additionally, comparisons were made for each integration step per day between DMSTA and \CRANpkg{DMSTAr}, with DMSTA results representing the reference for comparison.

Daily outputs for the 10-year period of simulation of discharge, total phosphorus load and water depth were compared against the reference within and between DMSTA and \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} comparisons. Multiple error statistics were calculated including normalized root mean square error (NRMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and maximum absolute error (Max Error; Supplemental Table S1). The NRMSE was selected as the primary convergence metric because it accounts for both bias and variance in the differences and is normalized by the reference mean to enable comparison across variables with different magnitudes MAE and max error were reported as secondary diagnostics to identify systematic bias and outlier behavior, respectively.

As an additional diagnostic, Richardson-style [@richardsonApproximateArithmeticalSolution1911] step-size convergence analysis was performed by fitting a power-law relationship to the NRMSE and integration t resolution on a log-log scale. Because DMSTA includes state-dependent constraints, threshold-based corrections, and discontinuous daily forcing, this analysis was used as an empirical diagnostic of step-size sensitivity rather than as a formal Richardson extrapolation to a continuous-time solution.  This approach has been applied to evaluate coupled system problems with stiff coupled systems in environmental models where step-size sensitivities and stability considerations arise due to modeling dynamics [@bayleyegnConvergenceMultipleRichardson2024; @gonzalez-parraCombinationNonstandardSchemes2010; @zlatevStabilityRichardsonExtrapolation2017; @zlatevEfficientImplementationAdvanced2022].

All model components were implemented in `R` (Ver 3.1.2, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna Austria), with functions organized to reflect hydrologic and biogeochemical process groupings. This design enables unit testing (\CRANpkg{testthat})[@wickhamTestthatGetStarted2011] , controlled experimentation, and integration with modern R workflows for data analysis and visualization. Model runs for \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} were performed serially (non-parallel) to eliminate variability from threading or task scheduling, consistent with the original model implementation.

# Results and discussion

## Model Translation

To verify that \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} is functionally equivalent to DMSTA, a diverse set of recent planning project simulations were evaluated. These scenarios included multiple network configurations and potential edge cases, providing a broad test of model behavior across representative applications. Agreement was evaluated at both the time-series scale and the annual performance-metric scale to ensure that \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} reproduced both short-term trajectories and long-term management-relevant outcomes. Across all tested configurations, \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} reproduced the legacy DMSTA model behavior with near-identical time-series trajectories and no systematic bias in long-term performance metrics (Table `r knitr::asis_output('\\@ref(tab:Tab2-tab)')`, Fig `r knitr::asis_output('\\@ref(fig:fig1)')`, `r knitr::asis_output('\\@ref(fig:fig2)')`, Supplemental Figures S1, S2, S3, S4, S5). Minor numerical differences were attributable to explicit time-stepping control, numerical precision, edge-case handling such as near-zero flows, or a combination of these factors, rather than changes to the underlying model formulation. Functional equivalence was therefore interpreted as reproduction of the same model behavior, trajectories, and performance metrics, rather than exact bitwise identity of every intermediate calculation.

The Bland–Altman analysis (Fig `r knitr::asis_output('\\@ref(fig:fig2)')`) indicated negligible systematic bias between DMSTA and \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} across all evaluated variables, with differences tightly clustered around zero and no evidence of magnitude-dependent divergence. The limits of agreement were small relative to the range of simulated values, supporting numerical equivalence between implementations. Similarly, low bias, small RMSE relative to the magnitude of annual outputs, and low median and 95th-percentile absolute percent differences further support high-fidelity reproduction of DMSTA by \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} (Table `r knitr::asis_output('\\@ref(tab:Tab2-tab)')`). Additionally, case (i.e., project and STA) specific bias and error estimates indicate a high degree of fidelity with most estimates being within 1% difference (Supplemental Table S2 and S3). The inclusion of low-flow and near-zero-flow conditions (i.e., edge cases) was important because these cases are most likely to expose differences in conditional logic, numerical safeguards, or rounding behavior between published DMSTA (MS Excel/VBA) results and \CRANpkg{DMSTAr}.

A key distinction between the two implementations is the computational environment in which the model is executed. DMSTA is a macro-driven Excel workbook in which model execution is orchestrated through VBA macros and depends heavily on worksheets, defined names, internal functions, cell references, and workbook state. DMSTA also relies on external project files that contain network configurations and input data. In contrast, \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} is a function-based R package that accepts inputs as data frames and/or lists and returns outputs as R objects, such as lists or data frames, rather than relying on workbook state. This design supports reproducible, code-based workflows that are easier to version control, test, document, and run in batch applications. As a result, \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} preserves the core DMSTA model formulation while providing a more transparent and extensible implementation for scenario analysis, sensitivity testing, and future model development. Although the evaluated scenarios covered a range of planning applications and network configurations, equivalence should continue to be verified when applying \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} to substantially different project configurations or future model extensions.

## Numerical Sensitivity and Stability

The numerical sensitivity analysis provides an important diagnostic of implementation fidelity between DMSTA and \CRANpkg{DMSTAr}. Because \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} was designed to reproduce the behavior of the original spreadsheet/VBA model rather than reformulate the underlying numerical method, the key question was not whether the model exhibited idealized theoretical convergence, but whether both implementations responded similarly to controlled changes in integration resolution. The results indicate that they did. Across discharge, total phosphorus load, and water depth, DMSTA and \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} produced nearly indistinguishable step-size error patterns when each implementation was compared with its own four-step-per-day reference simulation (Fig `r knitr::asis_output('\\@ref(fig:fig3)')`). This agreement indicates that the R implementation retained the numerical behavior of the original model and did not introduce additional step-size sensitivity.

```{r fig3, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5.5,fig.cap= "Step-size sensitivity of DMSTA and DMSTAr relative to the four-step-per-day reference simulation for STA 3/4 in the CEPP application. Error statistics are shown for normalized root mean square error (NRMSE; A–C), mean absolute error (MAE; D–F), and maximum absolute error (Max Error; G–I) for daily discharge, total phosphorus load, and water depth. Points show errors calculated independently for each implementation relative to its own four-step-per-day reference simulation."}

```

The convergence patterns were sublinear, with log–log slopes of approximately -0.51 for discharge and total phosphorus load and -0.50 for water depth when NRMSE was evaluated against steps per day. These slopes are lower than the theoretical values expected for idealized first- or second-order schemes derived for smooth, continuously differentiable systems [@hairerClassicalMathematicalTheory1993; @zlatevStabilityRichardsonExtrapolation2017]. In practice, reduced empirical convergence order is commonly observed in environmental models such as DMSTA with discontinuous forcing, threshold-based process switching, or stiff coupled dynamics, where the assumptions underlying classical error scaling are violated [@bayleyegnConvergenceMultipleRichardson2024; @zlatevEfficientImplementationAdvanced2022]. The model combines dynamic water and phosphorus mass-balance calculations with operational constraints, threshold-based corrections, and discontinuous daily forcing. These features can limit smooth error reduction with decreasing step size because changes in integration resolution may alter the timing or frequency of threshold crossings, operational adjustments, or state-dependent corrections. Consequently, the empirical error behavior reflects both numerical discretization and conditional model logic.

Differences between DMSTA and \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} were relatively stable across the integration resolutions tested  (Fig `r knitr::asis_output('\\@ref(fig:fig4)')`). If the R implementation had introduced a step-size-dependent numerical artifact, the difference between DMSTA and \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} would be expected to increase or decrease systematically as the number of integration steps per day changed. Instead, the magnitude of the DMSTA–\CRANpkg{DMSTAr} differences remained broadly similar across one, two, four, eight, and sixteen steps per day. This suggests that residual differences between the implementations are not primarily associated with temporal discretization. Rather, they likely arise from small implementation-level differences that are difficult to eliminate when translating a legacy spreadsheet/VBA model into a scripted R framework, such as rounding behavior, conditional evaluation order, or update sequencing.

```{r fig4, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5.5,fig.cap= "Direct comparison of DMSTA and DMSTAr across integration resolutions for during a limited simulation of STA 3/4 in the CEPP application. Error statistics are shown for normalized root mean square error (NRMSE; A–C), mean absolute error (MAE; D–F), and maximum absolute error (Max Error; G–I) for daily discharge, total phosphorus load, and water depth. Error statistics were calculated as DMSTAr minus DMSTA at each integration resolution."}

DMSTA_daily2 <- DMSTA_daily[,c("Date","WY","Nstep", "Q_out_total", "L_out_total","Depth")]
names(DMSTA_daily2) <- c("Date","WY","Nstep", "Q", "TPL","Depth")
DMSTA_daily2$method <- "DMSTA"

DMSTAr_daily2 <- DMSTAr_daily[,c("Date","WY","Nstep","Q_out_total","L_out_total","Z_end_cm")]
names(DMSTAr_daily2) <- c("Date","WY","Nstep", "Q", "TPL","Depth")
DMSTAr_daily2$method <- "DMSTAr"

DMSTA_DMSTAr_daily <- rbind(DMSTA_daily2,DMSTAr_daily2)|>
  melt(id.vars = c("Date","WY","Nstep","method"))|>
  dcast(Date+WY+Nstep+variable~method,value.var = "value",mean)

DMSTA_DMSTAr_daily$abs_error <- with(DMSTA_DMSTAr_daily,abs(DMSTAr - DMSTA))

error_Nstep_dmsta_dmstar <- ddply(DMSTA_DMSTAr_daily,c("variable","Nstep"),summarise,
      nrmse = 100 * sqrt(mean(abs_error^2))/mean(DMSTAr),
      mae = mean(abs_error),
      mad = median(abs_error),
      max_error = max(abs_error))


var_vals <- c("Q","TPL","Depth")
var_val_lab <- c("Discharge","Load","Depth")
par(mar=c(1.5,2.5,0.5,1),oma=c(2,2,1.5,0.25));
layout(matrix(1:9,3,3,byrow = TRUE))

xlim.val <- c(0,17);by.x <- 4; xmaj <- seq(xlim.val[1],xlim.val[2],by.x); xmin <- seq(xlim.val[1],xlim.val[2],by.x/2)
for(i in seq_along(var_vals)){
  tmp <- subset(error_Nstep_dmsta_dmstar,variable == var_vals[i])
  ymaj <- labeling::heckbert(min(tmp$nrmse),max(tmp$nrmse),3); ymin <- seq(min(ymaj),max(ymaj),min(diff(ymaj))/2)
  ylim.val <- range(ymaj)
  
  plot(nrmse~Nstep,tmp, type="n",
       ann = FALSE,axes = FALSE,ylim = ylim.val,xlim=xlim.val)
  abline(h = ymaj,v = xmaj, lty=3,col="grey",lwd=0.5)
  points(nrmse~Nstep,tmp,pch=21,bg = adjustcolor("dodgerblue1",0.5),cex = 1.25)
  axis_fun(2,ymaj,ymin,format(ymaj))
  axis_fun(1,xmaj,xmin,xmaj,line=-0.5)
  box(lwd=1)
  mtext(side=3,var_val_lab[i])
  if(i==1){
    mtext(side=2,line=3,"NRMSE")
  }
  mtext(side=3,adj=0.99,line=-1.25,LETTERS[i],font=2,cex = 1)
}
for(i in seq_along(var_vals)){
  tmp <- subset(error_Nstep_dmsta_dmstar,variable == var_vals[i])
  ymaj <- labeling::heckbert(min(tmp$mae),max(tmp$mae),3); ymin <- seq(min(ymaj),max(ymaj),min(diff(ymaj))/2)
  ylim.val <- range(ymaj)
  
  plot(mae~Nstep,tmp, type="n",
       ann = FALSE,axes = FALSE,ylim = ylim.val,xlim=xlim.val)
  abline(h = ymaj,v = xmaj, lty=3,col="grey",lwd=0.5)
  points(mae~Nstep,tmp,pch=21,bg = adjustcolor("dodgerblue1",0.5),cex = 1.25)
  axis_fun(2,ymaj,ymin,format(ymaj*1000))
  axis_fun(1,xmaj,xmin,xmaj,line=-0.5)
  box(lwd=1)
  if(i==1){
    mtext(side=2,line=3,"MAE (x1000)")
  }
  mtext(side=3,adj=0.99,line=-1.25,LETTERS[i+3],font=2,cex = 1)

}
for(i in seq_along(var_vals)){
  tmp <- subset(error_Nstep_dmsta_dmstar,variable == var_vals[i])
  ymaj <- labeling::heckbert(min(tmp$max_error)*0.9,max(tmp$max_error)*1.1,4); ymin <- seq(min(ymaj),max(ymaj),min(diff(ymaj))/2)
  ylim.val <- range(ymaj)
  
  plot(mae~Nstep,tmp, type="n",
       ann = FALSE,axes = FALSE,ylim = ylim.val,xlim=xlim.val)
  abline(h = ymaj,v = xmaj, lty=3,col="grey",lwd=0.5)
  points(max_error~Nstep,tmp,pch=21,bg = adjustcolor("dodgerblue1",0.5),cex = 1.25)
  axis_fun(2,ymaj,ymin,format(round(ymaj*10,2)))
  axis_fun(1,xmaj,xmin,xmaj,line=-0.5)
  box(lwd=1)
  if(i==1){
    mtext(side=2,line=3,"Max Error (x10)")
  }
  mtext(side=3,adj=0.99,line=-1.25,LETTERS[i+6],font=2,cex = 1)
 
}
mtext(side=1,outer=T,"Steps Per Day")

```

Overall, the numerical sensitivity analysis supports the use of \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} as a faithful implementation of DMSTA for the tested configuration. The model exhibited expected sensitivity to coarse temporal discretization, but this sensitivity was consistent between implementations. The sublinear convergence behavior reflects the complexity of the modeled system and the presence of threshold-based operations rather than instability introduced by the R implementation. These results provide additional confidence that differences between DMSTA and \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} are bounded, interpretable, and not strongly dependent on the selected integration step size.

# Conclusions

Collectively, these results indicate that \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} reproduced the numerical sensitivity of the original DMSTA implementation for the representative CEPP STA 3/4 simulation. The empirical convergence behavior was sublinear rather than first- or second-order, which is consistent with expectations for a model containing threshold-based operational logic, state-dependent corrections, and discontinuous daily forcing. Importantly, the step-size response was nearly identical in DMSTA and \CRANpkg{DMSTAr}, and the direct differences between implementations were relatively insensitive to the number of integration steps per day. Therefore, residual differences between DMSTA and \CRANpkg{DMSTAr} are unlikely to reflect numerical instability introduced by the R implementation. Instead, they likely represent minor implementation-level differences associated with translating a legacy spreadsheet/VBA model into a reproducible `R` framework.

\CRANpkg{DMSTAr} converts a widely used but difficult-to-audit treatment-wetland model into a transparent, modular, and reproducible ecological modelling framework. The package formalizes cell-scale hydrology and phosphorus dynamics, assembles cells into routed treatment networks, exposes intermediate states and fluxes for diagnostics, and supports scripted scenario and sensitivity analyses. Verification against established planning applications demonstrates that these gains in transparency and extensibility are achieved without materially altering legacy model behavior. More broadly, the framework illustrates how legacy ecological decision-support models can be translated into open, testable research software while retaining continuity with prior applications.
